en: Mayon Volcano emits toxic sulfur dioxide gas, so visitors must wear masks and stay outside its six-kilometer permanent danger zone.
Coastal towns near the Philippine Trench, like Legazpi, must practice tsunami evacuation drills when strong underwater earthquakes strike.
The Pasig River contains high levels of harmful bacteria, making swimming unsafe and requiring water treatment before drinking.
During the hot dry season, extreme heat index levels in Metro Manila can cause heatstroke, requiring students to drink water.
The steep slopes of the Cordillera mountains make provinces like Benguet highly prone to deadly landslides during heavy typhoons.
Stagnant water in abandoned tires around Mount Makiling breeds Aedes mosquitoes, which spread dangerous dengue fever to nearby communities.
The high altitude and clear skies of Baguio City expose visitors to stronger ultraviolet rays, making sunscreen necessary to prevent sunburn.
Taal Lake has underwater volcanic vents that release hot, toxic gases, making swimming in its Main Crater Lake strictly prohibited.
The Callao Caves in Cagayan have slippery, uneven limestone floors, so visitors must wear sturdy shoes and bring flashlights to avoid falls.
Touching the sharp fire coral reefs in Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park can cause severe skin burns and requires immediate first aid.
The Valley Fault System runs directly through Metro Manila, meaning residents must secure heavy furniture to walls to prevent earthquake injuries.
Contaminated floodwaters in Marikina City can spread cholera bacteria, so residents must always boil their drinking water after heavy typhoons.
